text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Labour Minister Norbert Bluem's plans for a reform of the pensions system meet widespread criticism.
- Government passes emergency legislation to slaughter 5,200 British and Swiss cattle amid fears about mad cow disease.
- Government predicts 1997 budget deficit of 2.9 percent of GDP, dangerously close to Maastricht limits.
- Employers want to propose their own reform of pensions system.
- Construction trade union determined to preserve current wage levels in sector.
HANDELSBLATT
- Deutsche Bank and Commerzbank chiefs tell their supervisory boards they plan unchanged dividends.
- Dollar breaks 1.65 deutschemark level.
- Row breaks out over fees charged by banks to customers of their competitors who use their cash machines.
- Four groups interested in buying Berlin utility Bewag.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Liberal Free Democrats (FDP), junior partners in ruling coalition, vows to block pension reform plans.
- Plans to tax life insurance could effectively devalue policies by around 15 percent, insurance companies say.
- Chancellor Helmut Kohl plans government statement on labour market situation for Friday.
- Tax investigators now employing private detectives in their hunt for tax dodgers, magazine says.
- Most branches of German industry enter 1997 with cautious optimism and plan to invest more than last year, survey says.
DIE WELT
- Government predicts unemployment will start to fall in May.
- Coalition's junior partners, the FDP and the Bavarain-based Christian Social Union (CSU), show opposition to Bluem's pension plans.
- Insurance sector vows to fight plans to tax life insurance.
- Government predictions in annual economic report meet with scepticism.
